title: Thread Tree
banner.nokey: No network key: frames are encrypted, only MAC-level data (addresses, RLOC16) is visible. Enter the Thread dataset in Settings.
banner.decrypt: Thread messages are received but cannot be decrypted: check the network key (dataset) and that the sniffer channel matches the network.
empty: No Thread nodes seen yet. Is the sniffer on the right channel?
filter: Filter or paste from Home Assistant (name, MAC, IPv6, RLOC16 …)
reach.direct.tip: The sniffer received frames transmitted by this node itself.
reach.indirect.tip: Known only from other nodes' traffic: the node is out of the sniffer's range. Addresses and mode may be incomplete; move or add a sniffer nearby.
legend.direct: Heard directly: the sniffer received frames from this node itself
legend.indirect: Indirect (dotted circle on the card): known only from other nodes' traffic, out of sniffer range; details may be incomplete
banner.waiting: The sniffer channel is unknown: enter the Thread dataset (it contains the channel and the network key).
banner.nosniffer: No sniffer stick found (USB 1915:154b) and no diagnostic stick either. Plug a stick in: it is used as soon as it appears.
sticks.title: USB sticks
sticks.sniffer.none: No sniffer stick plugged in (USB 1915:154b): no traffic, signal and behaviour data
sticks.diag.none: No diagnostic stick plugged in (USB 1915:cafe): no active diagnostics
sticks.help: Sticks are found by their USB identity and used as soon as they are plugged in: the sniffer for traffic and behaviour, the diagnostic stick for active diagnostics. Either one is enough.
set.name: Network name
set.help: Copy it from your border router, e.g. IKEA app: Hub settings → Thread network → More options → copy dataset; or `ot-ctl dataset active -x`. It contains the network key: treat it like a password.
set.note: Saving restarts the capture with the new key and channel. Already learned nodes are kept. The dataset is stored in a private file (mode 600) next to the database and is never sent back to the browser.
set.confirm.remove: Remove the stored dataset? The capture continues without a key.
set.locked.cli: The dataset was given on the command line or in the environment (THREAD_TREE_DATASET) and cannot be changed here.
set.locked.remote: Entering the dataset is restricted to the machine running Thread Tree (started with --local-config-only). Use an SSH tunnel (ssh -L 8787:localhost:8787 user@host) and open http://localhost:8787.
set.insecure: This connection is not encrypted (HTTP): the network key can be read by others on the network while you send it. Prefer an SSH tunnel to localhost on untrusted networks.
col.name: Name
d.name: Name
d.name.noext: This device is known only by its short address so far. If that address changes, the name may later end up on a different device; it is safest to name devices that show an extended address.
d.name.locked: Naming is restricted to the machine running Thread Tree (--local-config-only).
mac.unknown: Not known yet: so far the sniffer has only seen this device by its short address (RLOC16). The MAC address appears as soon as the device sends or receives a frame addressed with it, or attaches to a parent.
rebuild.tip: Forget the learned nodes and links and learn the network again; names are kept
header.diag.tip: Switch the background queries of the diagnostic stick on or off (it stays in the network)
log.clear.confirm:
Clear the log?

This deletes the history of every device and of the network, also in the database. Findings that count events of the last 24 hours (parent changes, gaps, restarts …) start again from zero. Devices, names, statistics and the dataset stay.
rebuild.confirm:
Rebuild the tree?

All learned nodes, links and addresses are cleared and learned again from live traffic. Routers reappear within minutes, sleepy devices can take much longer.

Names are kept (they are tied to the MAC address and reappear when the device is seen again). The Thread dataset is not touched.
rebuild.done: Tree cleared and rebuilding from live traffic. Names kept: {kept}; dropped: {dropped} (devices known only by short address).
online.indirect.tip: Never heard directly, but other devices keep sending frames to it. Weaker than "online": a device that just failed is still addressed for a while.
d.addressed.tip: Last frame another device sent to this one. Shows it is still being talked to, not that it answers.
d.name.viarloc: Since {since} this device has only been heard by its short address {rloc}, without a frame showing its MAC address. If the short address was handed to another device in the meantime without the sniffer noticing, the name may now be shown on the wrong device. This resolves itself when the device sends a frame with its MAC address again (e.g. when it re-attaches).
diag.card.routers.sub: of at most 32 in a Thread network
diag.card.capture.sub: {frames} frames in the last hour, {pct} decrypted
diag.findings.title: Findings
diag.findings.none: No findings: nothing noticeable in the data seen so far.
diag.note.passive: All values come from a passive sniffer and describe what it can hear. Findings are hints, not proof.
diag.nodes.title: Devices
diag.t.rssi_24h.tip: Average signal strength of the frames heard in the last 24 hours, measured at the sniffer
diag.t.bytes.tip: Size of the frames sent by this device, without the sniffer's own header; approximate
diag.t.retry.tip: Share of repeated frames: a sender repeats a frame when no acknowledgement arrives
diag.t.addressed.tip: Frames other devices sent to this device, counted even if the device itself is never heard
diag.t.adv.tip: Time between two MLE advertisements heard from this router; gaps over 2 minutes are ignored (missed frames)
diag.t.poll.tip: Time between two data polls of this sleepy device; gaps over 1 hour are ignored
diag.chart.rssi: Signal strength at the sniffer, last 24 hours
diag.chart.hist: Distribution of the RSSI measurements (red: weaker than -85 dBm)
diag.chart.activity: Frames per 10 minutes, last 24 hours (red: retransmitted)
diag.no_rssi: No signal data: the sniffer's metadata (TAP) is missing or the fields are not available in this Wireshark version.
diag.nosniffer: No values: the sniffer has not received a frame from this device (no sniffer connected, the device is out of its range, or only the active diagnostics are running). Signal, traffic and timing come from the sniffer.
diag.card.capture.none: No frame received: no sniffer connected (only active diagnostics) or wrong channel.
diag.note.sniffer: Measured at the sniffer's position: a device far from it looks weak and quiet without being so.
diag.links.none: No links known: this router's advertisements have not been heard, and no neighbour has reported a link to it.
legend.health: Coloured dot on a card: the Diagnosis view has a warning (orange) or a critical finding (red) for this device
legend.sev.info: a note: worth knowing, no action needed
legend.sev.warn: a warning: something to look at (in the log: a breach of the Thread standard or a loss)
legend.sev.crit: critical: the network or a central device is affected
legend.test.moved: the device attached to another router
legend.test.searching: the device searches for a parent
legend.test.waiting: no sign of the device since the start of the test
legend.csl: the device uses CSL (Thread 1.2 synchronized sleepy end device): its parent sends at agreed times, so it does not poll in a rhythm and the poll checks are skipped
diag.b.csl: synchronized sleepy end device: gaps in its polling are not judged
finding.offline.title: Offline
finding.offline.text: Not heard since {since}, longer than expected for its role.
finding.offline.hint: Check power supply and position. For a router, the devices attached to it ({children:device|devices} known) have to find another parent.
finding.single_link.title: Router with a single link
finding.single_link.text: Its only known link goes to {neighbor_node}. If that router or link fails, this router is cut off.
finding.single_link.hint: Place another router or repeater within its range. Only links from advertisements the sniffer heard are known, so a link may exist that was not seen.
finding.weak_links.title: All links weak
finding.weak_links.text: All known links of this router ({links}) have the lowest quality (LQ 1).
finding.weak_links.hint: Move it closer to another router or remove obstacles. LQ 3 means a link margin above 20 dB, LQ 1 only above 2 dB.
finding.asymmetric_link.title: Uneven link
finding.asymmetric_link.text: The link to {neighbor_node} is good in one direction and poor in the other ({lq_in} in, {lq_out} out).
finding.asymmetric_link.hint: Often an antenna orientation problem, interference at one side or a weaker transmitter. Reposition one of the two devices.
finding.critical_router.title: Critical router
finding.critical_router.text: If this router fails, {cuts_routers:other router|other routers} and {cut_children:device|devices} behind them lose their connection to the main mesh. {own_children:device is|devices are} attached to this router itself.
finding.critical_router.hint: Add a router that connects both sides. The result is based on the links known to the sniffer: a link it has not heard about makes this look worse than it is.
finding.adv_fast.title: Very frequent advertisements
finding.adv_fast.text: About {per_hour} MLE advertisements in the last hour, one every {mean} on average. A stable router sends one about every 30 seconds.
finding.adv_fast.hint: The timer restarts whenever the network changes. Frequent restarts point to an unstable neighbourhood (links appearing and disappearing, devices re-attaching) or a device that keeps rebooting.
finding.role_flap.title: Router changes address or role often
finding.role_flap.text: {count:change|changes} of role or short address in the last 24 hours.
finding.role_flap.hint: A router that disconnects and attaches again gets a new router ID. Look at its power supply, its links and the history below.
finding.unknown_parent.title: Parent unknown
finding.unknown_parent.text: It is not known which router this device is attached to.
finding.unknown_parent.hint: The parent becomes known from the device's data polls or when it attaches while the sniffer listens. Battery devices can take a while.
finding.parent_offline.title: Parent offline
finding.parent_offline.text: Its parent {parent_node} has not been heard for a long time.
finding.parent_offline.hint: The device has to find a new parent. If it stays offline, check the parent router first.
finding.reparenting.title: Changes parent often
finding.reparenting.text: {count:parent change|parent changes} in the last 24 hours.
finding.reparenting.hint: Typical for a weak link to its router or a device placed between two routers. A closer router or a better position usually helps.
finding.retry_high.title: Many retransmissions
finding.retry_high.text: {rate} of the {frames} frames heard in the last 24 hours were repeated because no acknowledgement arrived.
finding.retry_high.hint: Interference or a weak link between this device and its receiver. Check Wi-Fi on neighbouring channels, distance and obstacles. Measured at the sniffer, which can also miss acknowledgements.
finding.signal_weak.title: Weak signal at the sniffer
finding.signal_weak.text: Average {rssi} over {samples} measurements in the last 24 hours.
finding.signal_weak.hint: This is how the sniffer hears it, not necessarily how its neighbours do. If the device works fine, move the sniffer closer to get complete data from it.
finding.indirect_only.title: Not heard directly
finding.indirect_only.text: The sniffer only knows this device from other devices' traffic.
finding.indirect_only.hint: It is out of the sniffer's range. Addresses, mode and statistics stay incomplete. Move the sniffer closer to it.
finding.no_mac.title: MAC address unknown
finding.no_mac.text: Only the short address is known.
finding.no_mac.hint: The MAC address appears when the device sends a frame with it, or attaches while the sniffer listens. Naming such a device is risky because its short address can change.
finding.sniffer_silent.title: Sniffer receives nothing
finding.sniffer_silent.hint: Check the USB connection, the channel (it must match the network) and that the capture is running (status at the top).
finding.decrypt_failing.title: Messages cannot be decrypted
finding.decrypt_failing.text: {failed} Thread messages could not be decrypted, {ok} could.
finding.decrypt_failing.hint: Check the network key (dataset) and the channel. After a key change enter the new dataset in the Settings.
finding.partitions.title: More than one partition
finding.partitions.text: {count} partitions are active at the same time.
finding.partitions.hint: The network is split, for example after an outage of a border router. It normally merges again; if it stays split, look at the routers between the parts.
finding.no_border_router.title: No border router known
finding.no_border_router.text: No device was listed as a border router in the Network Data seen so far.
finding.no_border_router.hint: Network Data is sent rarely, so this can just mean 'not seen yet'. A border router connects Thread to your home network; without one Matter devices cannot be reached from outside.
finding.single_border_router.title: Only one border router
finding.single_border_router.hint: If it fails or is switched off, devices on this Thread network are unreachable from the home network. A second border router adds redundancy.
finding.router_limit.title: Router limit reached
finding.router_limit.hint: Thread allows at most {limit} routers; further router-capable devices stay end devices. That is normal, but the mesh cannot grow.
finding.router_near_limit.title: Close to the router limit
finding.router_near_limit.hint: Beyond {limit} routers new devices stay end devices. That is normal; the mesh just cannot grow further.
finding.leader_changes.title: Leader changes
finding.leader_changes.text: The leader role changed {count:time|times} in the last 24 hours.
finding.leader_changes.hint: A new leader is chosen when the old one disappears. Frequent changes point to an unstable device or link.
finding.many_offline.title: Many devices offline
finding.many_offline.hint: Check for a power outage or a problem at the sniffer (position, channel). If the sniffer is fine, look at the routers first: their children go offline with them.
finding.link_lossy.title: Router loses frames to a neighbour
finding.link_lossy.text: This router could not deliver {rate} of its frames to {neighbor_node} (no acknowledgement); it hears that neighbour at {rssi}. Messages lost even after repeating: {msg_rate}. Lossy links of this router: {links}.
finding.link_lossy.hint: The router measures this itself over its last frames, so it is a direct view of the link, unlike the sniffer's estimate. Typical causes: distance or obstacles, interference (Wi-Fi on a neighbouring channel, microwave, USB 3 devices) or a neighbour that is busy or restarting. Move one of the two routers or add a router in between.
finding.child_link_poor.title: Poor link to its parent
finding.child_link_poor.text: As its parent measures it: signal {rssi}, {rate} of the frames to the device not acknowledged, {msg_rate} of the messages lost.
finding.child_link_poor.hint: The parent counts the frames it sent to this device that were not acknowledged, and the messages lost even after repeating. About -90 dBm or weaker is close to the limit of what the radios can receive. Sleepy devices lose frames more easily because they only listen briefly after a poll. If the device is unreliable, move it closer to its parent or add a router nearby.
finding.child_age_high.title: Parent has not heard it for a long time
finding.child_age_high.text: Its parent last heard from it {age} ago; the parent drops a child after {timeout} of silence.
finding.child_age_high.hint: A sleepy device normally contacts its parent much more often. If it stays silent it is dropped and has to attach again (look for a new parent in the history). Check the battery, the position and the parent's link.
finding.router_no_detail.title: Router does not answer detail queries
finding.router_no_detail.text: Its child table and its neighbour table could not be read. Its children and links are known only from what other routers report.
finding.router_no_detail.hint: Routers with an older Thread stack (for example Thread 1.3 in some hubs) do not support these queries. Nothing is wrong with the router; signal and error rates of its links are missing from the diagnosis, except where the neighbouring routers report them.
finding.indirect_confirmed.title: Not heard directly, confirmed by diagnostics
finding.indirect_confirmed.text: The sniffer never received a frame from this device itself. The active diagnostics confirm it ({since}).
finding.indirect_confirmed.hint: Radio statistics (signal, retransmissions, timing) stay empty because they come from frames the sniffer receives. Addresses, mode, links and version come from the network itself. Move the sniffer closer to this device if you need the radio statistics.
finding.diag_failing.title: Active diagnostics not working
finding.diag_failing.hint: The statistics still come from the sniffer. Check the diagnostic stick (USB connection, port, firmware from docs/diagnostics.md) and that the dataset is entered. It tries again automatically.
finding.poll_gaps.title: Gaps in its polling
finding.poll_gaps.text: {count:gap|gaps} in the last 24 hours, the longest {longest}; usually it polls every {usual}. Its child timeout: {timeout}.
finding.poll_gaps.hint: A sleepy device has to contact its parent within its child timeout, otherwise the parent drops it and it has to search for a new parent; meanwhile it cannot be reached. Measured at the sniffer: if the device is weak at the sniffer, missed frames look like gaps. Gaps together with parent searches point to a poor link to its parent or to the battery.
finding.parent_searches.title: Searches for a parent
finding.parent_searches.text: {count:search|searches} for a parent (MLE Parent Request) in the last 24 hours.
finding.parent_searches.hint: A device searches when it has lost its parent: after a restart or battery change, or when its parent stopped answering. During the search it cannot be reached. Several searches a day mean the link to its parent keeps breaking: a router closer to the device or another position usually helps.
finding.poll_vs_timeout.title: Polls barely within its timeout
finding.poll_vs_timeout.text: It polls about every {usual}, its child timeout is {timeout}: one lost poll and its parent may drop it.
finding.poll_vs_timeout.hint: Thread requires a contact within the child timeout. These settings of the device leave no margin; that is a matter of its firmware. If it keeps dropping out, report it to the manufacturer.
finding.silent_now.title: Silent right now
finding.silent_now.text: No data poll for {seconds}, although it usually polls every {usual} and the sniffer hears other devices. Child timeout: {timeout}.
finding.silent_now.hint: If it stays silent beyond its timeout, its parent drops it. Check the device (battery, position). If it comes back by itself, the history shows the gap and whether it had to search for a parent.
finding.parent_choice.title: Chose a weaker parent
finding.parent_choice.text: When it last attached it chose {chosen} ({chosen_margin}), although {best} offered {best_margin} ({count:time|times} in 24 h).
finding.parent_choice.hint: The margins are what the routers measured when they answered its search. A device also weighs the parent's priority and connectivity, so a small difference is normal; 10 dB and more usually means a worse link than necessary. If it keeps dropping out, a restart near the better router lets it choose again.
finding.reboots.title: Restarted
finding.reboots.text: {count:restart|restarts} in the last 24 hours (its frame counter started again or skipped ahead).
finding.reboots.hint: A device keeps counting its secured frames across restarts and stores the counter ahead; a counter that starts again or jumps by a thousand means a restart or a reset. Frequent restarts point to the power supply (weak battery) or a firmware fault.
finding.supervision_missed.title: Parent did not supervise it
finding.supervision_missed.text: {count:time|times} in 24 hours its parent sent it nothing for longer than its supervision interval ({interval}); the longest gap {longest}.
finding.supervision_missed.hint: Since Thread 1.2 a parent must contact a silent child at least once per supervision interval, so the child notices a lost parent. Measured at the sniffer: frames it missed look like a gap. Repeated gaps point to the parent router (overloaded or old firmware).
finding.netdata_lag.title: Old Network Data
finding.netdata_lag.text: It advertised the old Network Data version {version} for more than 2 minutes while its partition already had {current} ({count:time|times} in 24 h).
finding.netdata_lag.hint: Network Data (prefixes, routes, services) spreads from the leader to all routers. A router that keeps an old version does not receive the updates; its devices may use stale routes. Check its links to the other routers.
finding.adv_gaps.title: Gaps in its advertisements
finding.adv_gaps.text: {count:gap|gaps} of at least 100 s without an MLE advertisement in 24 hours, the longest {longest}.
finding.adv_gaps.hint: A router advertises at least every 32 s (Trickle timer). Longer gaps while the sniffer heard others mean it was busy, restarting, or that its frames do not reach the sniffer reliably.
finding.attach_rejected.title: Did not accept attaches
finding.attach_rejected.text: {count:attach request|attach requests} of devices went unanswered in 24 hours.
finding.attach_rejected.hint: A router answers a Child ID Request with a Child ID Response. No answer means its child table is full or the frames got lost; the device then has to try another router.
finding.busy_sleepy.title: High radio activity for a sleepy device
finding.busy_sleepy.text: {per_hour} data polls in the last hour, the typical sleepy device here: {median}.
finding.busy_sleepy.hint: Every poll wakes the radio. Polling this often drains a battery much faster; it can be a setting of the device or a sign that it keeps waiting for data.
event.parent_choice: Chose parent {chosen} ({cm} dB) although {best} offered {bm} dB
event.netdata_lag: Old Network Data for {seconds}: version {version}, its partition has {current}
event.attach_unanswered: Router {router} did not answer its attach request
event.partitions.split: The network is split into {n} partitions
log.note: Device and network events as the sniffer (and the active diagnostics) recorded them, kept 30 days. Warnings: breaches of the Thread standard (parent choice, restarts, supervision, Network Data, advertisements, unanswered attaches, gaps beyond the child timeout) and losses (offline, leader change, split, border router or router lost).
event.parent_search: Searched for a parent (MLE Parent Request)
event.attached: Found a parent: {to} after {seconds} ({requests} Parent Requests)
diag.b.usual.tip: Median of the recent intervals between two data polls
diag.b.timeout.tip: As the device announced it when attaching: it must contact its parent within this time
diag.b.searches.tip: MLE Parent Requests: the device looked for a (new) parent
diag.chart.polls: Data polls per 10 minutes, last 24 hours (a gap shows as missing bars)
diag.note.behavior: Measured at the sniffer: a frame it missed looks like a frame that was not sent. Gaps only count while the sniffer kept hearing other devices.
tests.planned: More tests are planned, see "Planned tests" in the README.
tests.how: The program cannot switch, unplug or pair anything itself: you do that, it records what the network does. One test at a time; a test ends by itself after 30 minutes. Times are counted from the start of the test.
tests.router_outage.title: Router outage
tests.router_outage.desc: What happens when a router fails? Shows when it fell silent, whether the mesh dropped its links, and where and after how long its devices attached elsewhere.
tests.leader_outage.title: Leader outage
tests.leader_outage.desc: Without the leader the routers elect a new one after the network ID timeout (120 s by default), usually in a new partition. Shows how long that takes, the new leader and partition, and whether the Network Data was taken over.
tests.leader_outage.do: Now cut the power of the leader {name}.
tests.br_outage.title: Border router outage
tests.br_outage.desc: Shows when the border router's prefix and routes leave the Network Data and whether another border router takes over. Without one, Thread devices cannot be reached from the home network.
tests.br_outage.do: Now cut the power of the border router {name}.
tests.partition.title: Partition and merge
tests.partition.desc: Pick the router that connects two parts of the mesh (see "Critical router" in the findings). Shows whether the cut-off part forms a partition of its own and how long the parts take to merge again.
tests.partition.do: Cut the power of {name}, wait until a second partition shows up, then power it on again.
tests.router_upgrade.title: Router upgrade
tests.router_upgrade.desc: With fewer routers than the upgrade threshold (16 by default) a router-eligible end device should become a router when one fails. Shows whether and when that happens.
tests.router_upgrade.do: Now cut the power of {name} and wait a few minutes.
tests.router_return.title: Router comes back
tests.router_return.desc: Power a router on (or off and on again). Shows when it is heard and advertises again, whether it got its router ID back, and how many devices attach to it.
tests.router_return.do: Now power {name} on (if it is on: off for at least a minute, then on again).
tests.device_rejoin.title: Re-attach after a battery change
tests.device_rejoin.desc: Take the battery out of a device and put it back (or restart it). Shows the search for a parent, the number of Parent Requests, the chosen parent and the time until it is back.
tests.device_rejoin.do: Now take the battery out of {name} and put it back.
tests.commissioning.title: Commissioning a new device
tests.commissioning.desc: Start the test, then pair the new device with your app. Lists every device seen for the first time with its steps: discovery, parent search, attach. The encrypted joining itself (DTLS) cannot be followed.
tests.commissioning.do: Now pair the new device in your app.
tests.r.br_lost: it left the Network Data after {s}
diag.test.summary: {moved} of {n} devices moved to another router; the slowest after {longest}.
diag.test.no_children: No devices were attached to this router.
diag.test.note: Times are when the sniffer (or the active diagnostics) saw it, counted from the start of the test. A device far from the sniffer may move without being seen until the next round of the active diagnostics.
diag.active.off.sub: Only the sniffer is used. A second nRF52840 with OpenThread firmware adds what the routers measure themselves (docs/diagnostics.md).
diag.active.paused_note: Background queries are off: the stick stays in the network but asks nothing, so the active values grow old.
diag.active.switched_off: Active diagnostics switched off. The stick stays in the network.
diag.active.switched_on: Active diagnostics switched on: asking the network now.
diag.active.asked: Asking the network. The answers arrive within a minute.
diag.active.failures: {n:router|routers} did not answer the detail queries: {names}.
diag.note.active: Signal and loss values of links and children come from the routers themselves (active diagnostics); everything else comes from the passive sniffer. Findings are hints, not proof.
diag.self.tip: The stick that asks the network. It joined as an end device, so it shows up in the lists like any other device.
diag.sec.parentlink: Link to its parent (as the parent measures it)
diag.l.rss.tip: Average signal strength with which the parent receives this device
diag.l.margin.tip: Signal above the noise floor as the measuring device assumes it: above 20 dB is good, below 10 dB is weak. Chips assume different noise floors, so compare margins only between links measured by the same device.
diag.l.frame.tip: Share of the frames the parent sent to this device that were not acknowledged (moving average over the most recent frames)
diag.l.msg.tip: Share of the messages the parent could not deliver although it repeated every frame
diag.l.age.tip: Time since the parent last received anything from this device. The parent drops the device when this reaches the timeout.
diag.l.queued.tip: Messages the parent holds for this sleepy device until it asks for them
diag.l.supervision.tip: The parent checks on the device at this interval when it has been silent
diag.note.parentlink: Measured by the parent router, not by the sniffer; asked {ago}.
diag.link.note: Signal, margin and losses come from the router named under "Reported by": how it receives the neighbour, and how many of its frames to the neighbour were not acknowledged.
diag.children.note: Signal, losses and age are the parent's own measurements of each child (active diagnostics).
unknown-link: no known link to the leader
legend.edge.link: Router link; thicker line = better link quality
legend.edge.child: Attachment of an end device to its parent router
legend.edge.unknown: Dashed: relation unknown (no link information received yet)
legend.mesh.lq: Mesh view: colour and number of a link = link quality (3 green, 2 orange, 1 red; the weaker direction); arrowheads show the directions that work; faint = stale
legend.mesh.loss: Dashed line and ring: the router lost 25 % or more of its frames on this link (active diagnostics)
mesh.lq3: Link quality 3: good (more than 20 dB above the noise)
mesh.both: Arrowheads at both ends: frames get through in both directions
mesh.one: Arrowhead at one end only: frames get through only in that direction; the router at the arrowhead hears the other one, not the other way round
mesh.lossy: Dashed: a router loses 25 % or more of its frames on this link (active diagnostics)
legend.br: Border router: connects the Thread network to Wi-Fi/Ethernet; a device can have several addresses
legend.offline: Faded: not seen for longer than expected for this role
legend.source.derived: computed from the extended address / RLOC16 (always valid)

Thread: Low-power IPv6 mesh network protocol used by Matter devices.
RLOC16: Short address: router ID (upper 6 bits) + child ID (lower 9 bits). Changes when a device re-attaches; routers have child ID 0.
RLOC: IPv6 address built from the mesh-local prefix and the RLOC16; tells where a node is attached.
ALOC: IPv6 anycast address for a role, not a device: …:fc00 leader, …:fc10–fc1f the servers of a service (e.g. SRP), …:fc38 the primary backbone router.
ML-EID: Stable IPv6 address of a node inside the Thread network.
OMR: Address from a prefix that a border router advertises; reachable from outside the mesh.
LQ: 0–3 (3 = best) as reported by a router for a neighbor link.
BR: Device that connects Thread with other networks, e.g. IKEA DIRIGERA.
MTD: Never a router; end device only.
FED: FTD that currently is an end device. A REED (router-eligible end device) cannot be told apart passively.
MED: MTD whose radio is always on.
SED: MTD that sleeps and polls its parent (battery devices).
MLE: Thread control protocol; its advertisements reveal routers and links.
TLV: Encoding of data fields in Thread messages.
PAN: IEEE 802.15.4 network ID; one Thread network = one PAN ID.
RSSI: Strength of a received frame in dBm; closer to 0 is stronger (about -50 strong, -90 weak). Here: as received by the sniffer.
LQI: Quality value 0-255 that the radio reports for a received frame; derived from the chip, not comparable between chip vendors.
RSS: Signal strength in dBm as a Thread device measures it for a neighbour; the same quantity as RSSI, but measured by the network devices themselves instead of the sniffer.
REED: An end device that can become a router when the network needs one (passively indistinguishable from a FED).
SSED: Thread 1.2: a sleepy device that wakes at agreed times (CSL) instead of polling.
CSL: Thread 1.2: the parent sends to the child at agreed times; the child does not need to poll.
BBR: Thread 1.2: connects Thread to the home network for multicast and domain-wide addressing; the primary one answers ALOC …:fc38.
DTLS: Encryption used when a new device joins (commissioning); the sniffer cannot read it.
TAP: Metadata the sniffer adds to every frame: signal strength, link quality, channel.
ID: e.g. router ID (upper 6 bits of the RLOC16), partition ID, device ID.
HTTP: The (unencrypted) protocol of this web page.
SSH: Encrypted remote login; can tunnel this web page.
USB: How the sniffer and the diagnostic stick are connected.
WLAN: Wireless network on 2.4/5 GHz; on 2.4 GHz it can disturb Thread (channels 11-26).
dBm: Logarithmic unit of signal power: -70 dBm is stronger than -90 dBm.
MAC: Hardware address of the radio: the IEEE 802.15.4 extended address (EUI-64), 8 bytes, unique per device, shown like in Wireshark (aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff:00:11). Stays the same when the device re-attaches.
EUI-64: 64-bit hardware address (extended address) that identifies a node permanently.
SRP: Lets devices register services at the border router.
